title: How to talk an overpriced seller into a price reduction: a Mac guide for realtors
metaTitle: Talk an Overpriced Seller Into a Price Reduction, Mac Guide
description: Realtors: how to talk an overpriced seller into a price reduction using comps, days on market, and a short script you can reuse.
targetKeyword: talk an overpriced seller into a price reduction
intro: To talk an overpriced seller into a price reduction, start with data, not opinion. Pull recent sold comparables, note how many days each one took to sell, and compare that to the seller's listing. This page covers why listings go stale, what the wait costs, and fixes you can use this week without buying anything.
tldr: Use final sale prices from the last three months, not asking prices. Those show what buyers actually paid.
A listing that takes a week or more longer than its comparables' average days on market is a warning sign, per one Redfin agent's rule of thumb.
Lead with the seller's goal, then show the sheet. Ask before you argue.
Lazur can point at your comp columns, dictate your notes, and draft the email. You still check the numbers and press send.

blocks.text: Most overpriced listings do not fail loudly. They sit. Showings thin out, buyer feedback starts repeating the same concern, and the seller begins to blame the market, the photos, or you. Your job is to explain the gap before the seller decides the number is right.
Why overpriced listings go stale right now

Price cuts are common at the moment. Redfin reports that 21.1% of active U.S. listings had a price cut in the four weeks ending September 20, 2026. A year earlier the share was 19.8%. That is the highest share for that time of year since Redfin began tracking in 2022. The figure counts a flow of cuts, not a count of stale homes, so read it as a sign of pressure rather than a precise total.

Zillow shows the same pressure from another angle. Its July 2025 report found 27.4% of listings had a price cut, the largest share in its data back to 2018. The median listing lifespan that month was 60 days, four days longer than the pre-pandemic average. Listings that sold took 24 days. That gap is where an overpriced listing can end up.
What an overpriced listing costs the seller

The cost starts with fewer showings. Redfin notes that an overpriced listing can get fewer showings and longer listing times. Buyers may skip it, or compare it online and move on. An inflated price can also leave the appraisal short, so a deal can fall apart late. Each of those costs lands on the seller first, and then on you.

blocks.text: Read the Indiana numbers with care. The analysis treats each final sale price as true market value, and the authors say that may not hold for every listing. It also shows a timing pattern. Homes with one price reduction spent a median 23 days at the original price before the cut. They went under contract a median 12 days after the cut. Homes with no reduction went under contract in a median 5 days.

A 2017 study in the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics looked at 13,461 single-family sales. Of those, 4,308 had a listing price reduction. The authors found that overpricing often leads to a reduction. They estimated the effect of a listing price change on net selling price at two to three times the size of the reduction. Treat that as a warning, not a formula. It covers one set of sales and measures a relationship, not a guarantee.
Your time is part of the cost

Stale listings also cost you hours. NAR's 2026 Member Profile puts the median Realtor at 35 hours of work per week, unchanged from the prior year. An overpriced listing adds price calls, extra showing follow-ups, and repeated comp checks. None of that shows up on the listing sheet, but all of it comes out of the same week.

NAR's 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers gives the baseline, as summarized by Virginia REALTORS. Recently sold homes spent a median four weeks on the market, one week longer than the year before. The median seller sold for 99% of list price. The typical seller did fine near list. The overpriced ones are the sellers you need to reach before the wait grows.
Build the case before the seller call

Start with the right comparables. Redfin advises basing list price on recently sold comparables, meaning final sale prices, not asking prices. In a changing market, use sales from the last three months that you would honestly compete against. Leave out the sales you wish you could be compared with. Keep the ones a buyer would really consider.

items: Pull sold comparables from the last three months. Use final sale prices, and skip homes you would not honestly compete against.
Write each comparable's days on market in one column, next to its sale price.
Calculate the average days on market for the comparables. In Google Sheets, type =AVERAGE( and select that column.
Write down your listing's days on market and how many showings it has had.
Compare the two averages. Redfin's rule of thumb: a week or more longer than the comparables' average points to overpricing.
List the buyer feedback you have heard, and count how often price came up.

blocks.text: Turn the numbers into a short conversation

Ask the seller what they need before you show them anything. Ask about timing, about the move they are planning, and about the net they expect. Then show the sheet. Let the comparables do most of the arguing. Your role is to read the numbers out loud and say what they mean for this listing.

A simple script helps. Open with the goal, then the evidence, then the choice. You might say that the listing has been on the market longer than recent comparables, that buyers keep raising price, and that you can either hold the price with a re-test date or reduce it now. Two clear options beat one ultimatum.
Mistakes that make the talk fail

items: Arguing from opinion. A seller can wave off a gut feeling in one sentence. Sold data is harder to brush aside.
Using asking prices as proof. Asking prices show what owners hope for, not what buyers paid. Use final sale prices.
Waiting until the listing is old. NAR's averages rise from 4.9% for 0 to 14 days on market to 13.8% after 120 days, though the article does not state the basis.
Pasting client details into a tool your brokerage has not approved. Check your brokerage's rules on client data first.
Forgetting the appraisal. An inflated price can leave the appraisal short. Say so early, before an offer exists.

blocks.text: Some listings do not fit the pattern. If you have few recent sales, say so. Thin comparables make any average shaky. A property with unusual features, such as a large lot or an odd layout, may not compare well with simple sales. In those cases, show the range of recent sales and explain what they cannot tell you. Admitting limits builds trust with a seller who has heard many confident pitches.

Before you paste seller details into any AI tool, follow your brokerage's rules and your state's rules on client data. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. The audio and screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your brokerage's policy still comes first.
Where to start this week

If your comparables live in a spreadsheet, start with the Google Sheets guide for realtors on Mac at /for/realtors/google-sheets. For the seller email, the Gmail guide at /for/realtors/gmail covers templates and scheduled send. The routine in the plan above works with either one, and you can run it with nothing new installed.

Keep a copy of your comparables in the listing file. When the seller asks again in a month, you can show what changed instead of starting over. faq.question: Can I refuse to list a home at a price I think is too high?
faq.answer: The seller sets the price. Your job is to advise with evidence and keep that advice in writing. Check your brokerage's policy on pricing advice before you go further, and follow it.

faq.question: How many comparables should I use?
faq.answer: Redfin's guidance does not give a fixed count. It says to use recent sales you would honestly compete against, and in a changing market to use sales from the last three months. Fewer strong sales beat many weak ones.

faq.question: Is the 21.1% figure the share of stale listings?
faq.answer: No. Redfin's 21.1% is the share of active U.S. listings that had a price cut in the four weeks ending Sept 20, 2026. It measures a flow of cuts. It does not count how many listings are stale.

faq.question: What if the seller says the market is just slow?
faq.answer: Show the sold data and the days on market for each comparable. Redfin says balanced-market homes typically sell within 30 to 90 days. Place the listing against that range and the comparables' average, then let the seller see the gap.

faq.question: Does a price cut always help a listing sell?
faq.answer: No. The Indiana analysis is correlational and does not prove that earlier cuts cause faster sales. The Gordon and Winkler study measures a relationship between price changes and net selling price. Present both as evidence, not as a promise.

faq.question: Can Lazur send the email or change my listing for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and types text, points at things on your screen, and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. You read the draft, then send it yourself.

costs.title: Time on the market
costs.text: Redfin says an overpriced listing can get fewer showings and longer listing times. Zillow's July 2025 data put the median listing lifespan at 60 days. Track your own listing against its comparables, not only against that national median.

costs.title: A lower final price
costs.text: The 2017 Gordon and Winkler study estimated the effect of a listing price change on net selling price at two to three times the size of the reduction. A late cut can cost the seller more than the number on the sheet suggests.

costs.title: Your week
costs.text: NAR's 2026 Member Profile puts the median Realtor at 35 hours of work per week. A stale listing adds calls, follow-ups, and comp rechecks to that week. Those hours never appear on the commission sheet.

costs.title: Deal risk at appraisal
costs.text: An inflated price can leave the appraisal short. Redfin says that can make the deal fall apart. That loss is time and effort as well as money, so raise appraisal risk early, not after an offer.

causes.title: Pricing from asking prices, not sales
causes.text: Asking prices show what an owner hopes to get. They do not show what buyers paid. Redfin's pricing guidance says to base list price on recently sold comparables, meaning final sale prices, not asking prices. A list price built on asking prices starts from a number nobody has paid.

causes.title: Starting from the first number the owner wants
causes.text: Sellers often start from the price they paid, a neighbor's sale, or the amount they need. Gordon and Winkler found that homes with listing price changes had original prices about 18% higher than unchanged homes. That gap narrows to about 9.7% when you compare final listing prices. The first number is often the one that causes the trouble.

causes.title: Comparables that flatter the house
causes.text: Picking sales from a bigger or nicer street makes a price look reasonable. Redfin says to use sales you would honestly compete against. If the house needs work or sits on a busier road, the comparables should reflect that, even when the seller would rather they did not.

causes.title: A market that changed under the listing
causes.text: In a changing market, older sales can mislead. Redfin, quoting Brett Mansfield, advises using sales from the last three months that you would honestly compete against. A listing priced on last year's sales may be out of step with what buyers pay now.

causes.title: Ignoring buyer feedback
causes.text: Redfin lists warning signs for overpricing: fewer showings, repeated price concerns, and nearby homes selling while yours does not. When buyers raise price again and again, treat it as data, not as noise to explain away.

causes.title: Waiting for the seller to ask about price
causes.text: Agents sometimes wait for the seller to raise the price question. By then the listing has used up its freshest weeks. In Indiana's data, homes with one reduction spent a median 23 days at the original price first. Raise the question early, while the listing is still new.

fixes.title: Pull sold comps from the last three months
fixes.text: Use your MLS or any sold data you already have access to. Keep only final sale prices, not asking prices. In a changing market, the last three months give the closest picture. Put each sale on its own row with the address, sale price, and days on market.

fixes.title: Compare days on market, not just price
fixes.text: Check each comparable's days on market, then find the average. Redfin's agent John Myers uses a simple rule. If your listing takes a week or more longer than the comparables' average, that points to overpricing. Balanced markets typically sell homes within 30 to 90 days, so use that range as a second check.

fixes.title: Build the sheet in Google Sheets or Numbers
fixes.text: In Google Sheets, select the comp list and go to Data > Pivot table to group sales by month or street. Apple's Numbers guide describes formulas, filters, grouping, pivot tables, and charts that update when table data changes. Either app works for a one-page comp sheet.

fixes.title: Check your listing the way a buyer does
fixes.text: Search for your own listing the way a buyer would, then look at the nearby homes that sold. Redfin notes that buyers may compare online and move on. If nearby homes are selling while yours is not, you have a signal worth sharing with the seller.

fixes.title: Ask questions before you give an answer
fixes.text: Ask the seller about timeline, the move they are planning, and the net they expect. Write those answers down in the sheet. Then show the data that fits those goals. Sellers hear a recommendation better after they feel heard.

fixes.title: Offer two clear options
fixes.text: Hold the price with a set re-test date, or reduce it now. Two options give the seller something to decide. A single demand leaves the seller with only a yes or a no. Write both options in a short email so the seller can reread them.

fixes.title: Set a recheck date in Reminders
fixes.text: Create an Apple Reminders entry for the day you will recheck the comps and showings. Reminders supports adding dates to reminders. Paste the link to the comp sheet into the reminder's notes so you can open it in one step.

fixes.title: Draft the follow-up email before the call ends
fixes.text: Write a short email with the comps and your recommended option. Keep the numbers in the email the same as the numbers on your sheet. Send it after the seller confirms the call, not before. A saved template can keep the layout for next time.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Pull the comps
plan.text: Pull sold comparables from the last three months. Keep final sale prices only. Put each sale on its own row in Google Sheets, with the sale price and days on market.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Measure the gap
plan.text: Average the comparables' days on market. Compare your listing's days on market to that average. Count showings and write down buyer feedback about price.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Write the talking points
plan.text: Write three lines: the seller's goal, the evidence, and two options. Hold fn to dictate a rough version into a note. Ask Lazur to explain any term you are unsure of.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Hold the seller call
plan.text: Ask about the seller's timeline and goals first. Then show the sheet. Let the seller respond before you give your recommendation.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Send the follow-up and set a recheck
plan.text: Send a short email with the two options. Create a Reminders entry for the recheck date, with a link to the comp sheet in its notes.
